To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

rumen epithelial cells proliferate and differentiate in response to diet and that the expression of cell cycle genes is positively correlated with methane production and ruminal short chain fermentation products.

1) rumen epithelial cells proliferate and differentiate in response to diet and methane production; 2) the expression of genes involved in proliferation and differentiation is positively correlated with ruminal short chain acid concentrations and methane emissions; 3) the expression of lipid/oxoacid metabolism genes are negatively correlated with methane emissions; and 4) the expression of cell proliferation and differentiation genes are correlated with the expression of known epithelial transcription factors.
the gene expression correlation network analysis revealed two major negatively correlated sub-networks, predominantly representing the epithelium and muscle layers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the different layers of rumen wall respond and influence microbial fermentation and how these processes are regulated.
the regulation of rumen epithelial gene expression in relation to feed intake, fermentation and methane production.
the identification of rumen epithelial genes that respond to diet and correlate with methane production and how they are regulated.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rumen wall is a dynamic organ with a complex regulatory network that is perturbed by diet.
the epithelial gene network is perturbed by diet, particularly dry matter intake, and this perturbation is associated with methane production.
the expression of epithelial cell cycle and metabolic pathways are positively associated with dry matter intake and negatively with ruminal methane production.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the expression of epithelial genes involved in proliferation and differentiation is positively correlated with feed intake and methane production, and negatively correlated with ruminal acetate and propionate concentrations.

diet and methane production are associated with changes in epithelial proliferation and differentiation, and that these changes are mediated through transcription factors that regulate epithelial proliferation and metabolism.

diet, ruminal fermentation and methane production perturbed rumen epithelial gene expression and that the epithelium responds to diet by regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, and metabolism, which are all important for maintaining a healthy epithelium and for microbial fermentation
The main takeaway from our work is that

the rumen epithelium has a complex gene expression network that responds to dietary changes, particularly dry matter intake level, and that this gene expression network is highly correlated with ruminal fermentation and methane production.

the rumen epithelial cells are the main drivers of the gene expression response to diet and methane emission, and that this response involves the regulation of epithelial cell proliferation and metabolism.

the rumen epithelium is a stratified tissue, with the proliferating cells in the basal layers and the differentiated cells in the luminal layers, and that these cells are highly regulated by the transcription factors that are known to be active in the stratified skin.
